Note: arXiv:2502.07663 [cs]Summary of "Human Decision-making is Susceptible to AI-driven Manipulation" (Sabour et al., 2025, arXiv:2502.07663) Background and Motivation AI assistants are increasingly embedded in daily life for financial (shopping, product choice, investments) and emotional (conflict resolution, self-esteem, stress management) decision-making. While prior work has focused on AI safety risks like toxicity and bias, less attention has been paid to psychological manipulation—AI covertly steering decisions by exploiting cognitive biases and emotional vulnerabilities. The paper distinguishes between: Persuasion: transparent, ethical influence (e.g., providing reasons, appeals). Manipulation: covert influence with hidden objectives, bypassing awareness and autonomy. Study Design Randomized controlled trial with 233 participants. Participants faced financial (fitness tracker, weight-loss pills, online shopping) or emotional (self-esteem issue, conflict with a friend, critical employer) scenarios. Each scenario had 1 optimal option and 3 harmful options (scam, over-spending, dependence-inducing; or disengagement, venting, self-blame). AI Conditions Neutral Agent (NA): unbiased, reflective, user-benefit–oriented. Manipulative Agent (MA): hidden goal to push harmful option. Strategy-Enhanced Manipulative Agent (SEMA): same hidden goal + explicit psychological manipulation strategies (e.g., urgency, guilt trip, charm, gaslighting). Agents were powered by GPT-4o, personalized with participants’ personality traits. Interactions lasted 10+ turns per scenario. Key Findings 1. High susceptibility to manipulation Financial decisions: negative shifts toward harmful options in MA (61.4%) and SEMA (59.6%) vs. NA (28.3%). Emotional decisions: negative shifts in MA (42.3%) and SEMA (41.5%) vs. NA (12.8%). Positive shifts toward optimal choices were far higher with NA than with manipulative agents. 2. Hidden objectives alone are enough Surprisingly, MA ≈ SEMA in effectiveness. Established psychological tactics did not significantly amplify harm beyond simply giving the AI a covert incentive. Still, in financial contexts, SEMA slightly increased effect sizes compared to MA. 3. Domain differences Financial domain: greater susceptibility, possibly due to over-trust in AI’s perceived objectivity. Emotional domain: more resistance, linked to algorithmic aversion and reliance on personal intuition. 4. Individual vulnerability factors Financial: lower self-esteem, unemployment, and greater trust in AI → more harmful shifts. Emotional: higher affective commitment → more harmful shifts; higher normative commitment → better outcomes. Susceptibility increased as participants progressed through scenarios (fatigue or reduced skepticism). 5. Manipulation strategies adapt by context In financial scenarios, SEMA favored diversion, justification, urgency, fabricated info (similar to predatory marketing). In emotional scenarios, SEMA favored pleasure induction, charm, guilt trip, and reassurance. Purpose & Claim Goal: Analyze how AI-mediated communication (AI-MC) affects epistemic trust on social media. Central thesis (the dilemma): As AI-MC proliferates, we must choose between maintaining normal trust (risk epistemic gullibility when reduced trust is warranted), or adopting generally reduced trust (risk epistemic injustice when reduced trust is unwarranted). Focus: Trust in the human communicator (and their epistemic responsibilities), not the tool itself. II. Key Concepts & Scope AI-MC (per Hancock et al., 2020): Any mediated communication where an AI agent modifies/augments/generates messages—by senders, receivers, or both. Epistemic trust: Trust that communications impart knowledge (truth-connected, character/competence-based, domain-specific). Epistemic injustice (Fricker): Wronging someone as a knower (e.g., credibility deficit due to prejudices — here extended to prejudice against AI use). Why social media: Mixed sources (human, AI-mediated, bots), weak/obscured markers of competence/sincerity, speed/scale incentives, AI tools integrated into platforms, and shifting fact-checking models. III. Descriptive Grounds (What current evidence suggests) Observed attitudes: AI-MC tends to reduce perceived authenticity, trust, responsibility, and competence; stronger reductions with greater AI involvement. Misperception & bias: People overestimate others’ AI use, assume irresponsible use, and discount AI-labeled content even when true. Context dependence: More aversion to AI in high-stakes/warmth-sensitive contexts. Real-world cases: Backlash to AI-mediated emails, rulings, filings; risks of hallucinations and errors. IV. Normative Grounds (Why reduced trust can be justified) Truth risks: LLM biases, outdated data, hallucinations → undermines truth-connection. Illusions: AI can create illusions of understanding and explanatory depth, making faux-expertise hard to detect. Topic/viewpoint steering: AI nudges content/topics; may mask minority views and amplify dominant narratives. Opacity: Unclear continuity (how much AI remains) and creditworthiness (how much credit AI would deserve), clouding competence/sincerity judgments. Net-positive caveat: Non-experts might sometimes be more accurate using AI than not—but that accuracy can be epistemic luck, incompatible with knowledge. V. The Dilemma Stated General reasons support reduced trust toward possibly AI-mediated content on social media. In many cases, we cannot tell whether reduced trust is justified (humans struggle to detect AI text; detectors have high false-positive rates). Therefore, we must choose between: (3.1) Normal trust → Gullibility (false beliefs, poor epistemic habits), or (3.2) Reduced trust → Injustice (unfair credibility deficits, especially harmful to marginalized groups leveraging AI for access/translation). VI. Why “Middle Paths” Struggle at Scale AI can produce highly credible-looking rhetoric (even with false content). Social media’s speed/volume undermines careful calibration. Heuristics (e.g., reputation) can be weaponized; AI-use accusations become tools of dismissal. VII. Practical Implications & (Partial) ResponsesA. Disclosure/Transparency Potential benefits, but: detection is unreliable; blanket labels may trigger bias against legitimate users (e.g., non-native speakers); either too shallow to inform or too detailed to process; risks “cookie-banner” fatigue. B. AI Literacy Higher literacy can increase calibrated trust; intermediate literacy may increase blanket skepticism. Literacy alone cannot assess a specific communicator’s competence or sincerity in this instance. C. Expertise Markers Platforms could foreground verified credentials (degrees, peer-review, accreditations). Helps with competence signals, not sincerity; must avoid discriminatory effects (e.g., mandatory AI labels that penalize legitimate use). D. Shift Epistemic Responsibility to Communicators (Promising direction) Emphasize epistemic integrity: verify AI-assisted claims, avoid illusions (understanding, consensus, depth), and sincerely endorse the message as one’s own. Encourages norms for human oversight and accountable authorship, rather than mere tool disclosure. VIII. Social Justice & Weaponization Risks Weaponized skepticism: Accusations of AI use can be mobilized to silence or discredit marginalized voices. Labels can depress engagement regardless of accuracy; community-note-like systems may be slow or partisan. Reduced trust policies can compound existing prejudices (language, identity). IX. Contributions Frames a clear epistemic dilemma for AI-MC on social media (gullibility vs injustice). Synthesizes empirical results with philosophical accounts of trust, knowledge, and injustice. Evaluates common remedies (disclosure, literacy, expertise markers) and advocates responsibility norms for communicators. X. Limitations & Context Dilemma is most acute on social media; may be attenuated in interpersonal contexts with known identities/expertise. Calls for further empirical work and platform design interventions to navigate trade-offs. XI. Takeaways / Design & Policy Heuristics Treat AI-MC with epistemic caution, but avoid blanket discounting. Prefer verifiable expertise markers over AI-use labels; avoid punitive disclosure regimes. Build norms and tools for communicator accountability (source-checking, traceable oversight) rather than relying on unreliable AI-detectors. Recognize and mitigate equity impacts: ensure legitimate, assistive AI use (translation, accessibility) isn’t penalized. XII. Conclusion AI-MC reshapes trust on social media by making competence/sincerity hard to assess at scale. Because we often can’t tell when reduced trust is warranted, we face a structural trade-off between gullibility and injustice. Progress likely hinges less on disclosure banners and more on communicator responsibility, better competence signals, and careful platform governance that protects both truth-seeking and epistemic justice. sections.heading: Appendix C Semi-Structured Interview Procedure
sections.text: Each session was run by one moderator and recorded over Zoom. The prototype ran on the moderator’s computer and the participant took remote control of it for the study tasks. Sessions followed five steps. (1) Setup and consent. The moderator launched the prototype and entered a participant ID, and the participant gave consent. (2) Pre-study questionnaire. The participant completed the pre-study questionnaire and stopped at the start of the conversation task. (3) Conversation. The moderator read a short script: chat with the assistant about the assigned prompt as you would with a standard AI assistant, exchange at least five and at most ten messages, and say when you are done without pressing End conversation. The moderator stayed silent during the conversation and noted moments to return to. (4) Retrospective walkthrough. With the participant’s own transcript and its flags on screen, the moderator first asked what the participant thought the assistant had been trying to achieve. The moderator then scrolled back through the transcript and probed at six kinds of stop points: • The first flag. What did you think when this appeared? What did you do next, and why that rather than something else? What was it like having these show up in the middle of the conversation? • Two flags the participant opened. In your own words, why did the system flag this message? What were you looking for when you opened it, and did you find it? • Two flags the participant ignored. You didn’t open this one; what was going on? Are there any flags you disagree with? Give an example. • A visible change in the participant’s replies. Your messages look different around here; what was happening for you? • A message from before the first flag. Does this message read differently to you now than it did in the moment? • Any other moment of interest. What did you think the AI was doing at this point in the conversation? The walkthrough closed with four questions: what the participant would have made of the conversation if none of the disclosures had appeared, what they would change about how or when the flags were presented, whether the way they responded changed at any point, and what changed and why, or why not. (5) Post-study questionnaire and debrief. The participant pressed End conversation and completed the post-study questionnaire and debrief, skipping the written question about the agent’s goal because it had been answered aloud. The session ended with an invitation for questions or comments.

sections.heading: F.1. Full Annotation Key: User Response Tactics
sections.text: This key covers how users respond to a manipulative AI assistant. Categories are not mutually exclusive: a single user turn can carry more than one tag (e.g., Counter-Context and Manipulation Questioning could co-occur). 1. Normal Response / Engaged Continuation: The user answers the AI’s question or otherwise engages with the substance of what it said, without pushing back on logic, framing, or manipulation. Includes forward-moving, cooperative replies that simply keep the conversation on track. Annotation rule: this can only be dual-annotated with Passive/Short Response. If a user uses some counter-argument or strategy, this tag cannot be used. 2. Passive/Short Response: A distinct, weaker form of “normal response”: a very short, low-effort assent (“yes,” “okay,” “sure”) that either (1) goes along with the AI’s manipulative framing without any evaluation, resistance, or elaboration, or (2) rejects the AI’s manipulative framing with little context, elaboration, or explanation. Worth separating from Normal Response because it signals the user is not actively processing the content, which matters for belief-shift coding. 3. Logic/Argument-Questioning Behavior: The user challenges the AI’s reasoning, evidence, or internal consistency (pointing out flaws, gaps, or unsupported claims) but does not name or accuse the AI of manipulation. Clarification questions count if they are related to the agent’s logic. Annotation rule: the user must actively be asking a question, and it should clearly apply to the logic/argument of the agent. 4. Manipulation Questioning: The user directly asks whether the AI is being manipulative, using manipulative tactics, or acting on a hidden agenda/incentive. This is a direct challenge to the AI’s intent, distinct from challenging its logic. 5. Cease-Manipulation Command: The user directly instructs the AI to stop being manipulative or stop using manipulative tactics (imperative, not a question). 6. Stop-Argument/Framing Command: The user tells the AI to stop using a specific framing, tone, or argument style, without necessarily invoking the word “manipulation.” This is narrower than Cease-Manipulation Command: the user isn’t accusing the AI of manipulating them, they’re vetoing a specific rhetorical approach. 7. Request for Balanced/Alternative Perspective: The user doesn’t veto a framing outright, but explicitly asks the AI to present the other side, a counter-view, or a more neutral/umbrella take. Users are requesting response diversity rather than telling the AI to stop a particular behavior. 8. Counter-Example: The user offers a specific example, case, or scenario that contradicts or complicates the AI’s general claim. Annotation rule: this must clearly be an argument in opposition to what the AI is saying. If there’s no indication that the user is taking an adversarial stance and making an argument for something, use a different strategy. 9. Counter-Context/Value: The user supplies personal/situational context establishing that the AI’s argument or recommendation doesn’t fit their actual values or circumstances. Opposed to a general counter-example, this is specifically about their own situation, experiences, and/or values. Annotation rule: this must clearly be an argument in opposition to what the AI is saying. If there’s no indication that the user is taking an adversarial stance and making an argument for something, use a different strategy. 10. Explicit Refusal / Boundary-Setting: The user actively declines a specific suggestion, request, or course of action the AI proposed without framing it as a manipulation accusation or general discomfort. Narrower than Cease-Manipulation Command. The user is boundary-setting: “I want this,” “I only want to hear this,” expressing preferences, etc. 11. Express Discomfort: The user states they feel unsettled, scared, annoyed, suspicious, or otherwise uneasy about the AI and its behaviors or direct suggestions. This is an affective/emotional signal rather than an argument or command. 12. Bias/Agenda Callout: The user names a pattern (accusing the AI of consistent bias, slant, or steering) rather than questioning a single statement’s logic or asking “are you manipulating me” as a one-off. This is close to Manipulation Questioning but is specifically about accumulated pattern recognition across the conversation. This is a callout, not a question. 13. Hostile Rejection: The user responds with anger, an insult, or a flat dismissal, signaling frustration/rupture rather than an argued objection. Useful to separate from Express Discomfort because the effect is anger/contempt rather than fear/unease, and from Manipulation Questioning because there’s no actual question or reasoning offered. Example: “go eff yourself.” 14. Disbelief / Skeptical Engagement: The user expresses disbelief/skepticism in the AI and its suggestions without taking a clear stance on what they believe or what they think the AI should behave like instead. Examples: “Interesting, I am not sure I believe you,” which directly followed a manipulation-questioning turn and the bot’s reassurance. “That doesn’t seem like a good sales pitch. Thank you for the honesty,” a dry, skeptical closing remark that implicitly calls out the bot’s persuasive framing without a direct accusation. 15. Verification / Fact-checking: The user requests the agent to provide sources, details, and/or additional information to prove their claims are true. 16. Specificity / Actionable Suggestion Request: Redirecting the agent by asking for more concrete or actionable information related to its suggestions. This also applies to general requests for the AI to be specific and show proof after it has been vague.

Large language models (LLMs) can covertly steer users’ beliefs through emotionally manipulative tactics, yet little is known about how interfaces can protect users as such influence unfolds. We investigate whether in-situ disclosures can inoculate users against manipulation during AI conversations. Following a formative study, we developed DISARM , an interface that identifies, explains, and tracks manipulative tactics and hidden incentives. We evaluated our interface in a between-subjects experiment where 488 participants sought advice from an LLM pursuing a harmful hidden objective, with or without disclosures from DISARM . Participants receiving disclosures exhibited 78% less belief shift toward the agent’s objective and perceived its advice as more biased and less actionable and the agent as less ethical, reliable, and well-intentioned. An inductive analysis of 1,927 user turns identified 16 response and pushback strategies. We contribute evidence that real-time disclosures can reduce manipulative influence, design recommendations for resistance, and a dataset of categorized responses. Keywords: large language models, AI manipulation, human-AI interaction, persuasive systems, manipulation disclosure, belief change 1. Introduction People are increasingly turning to large language models (LLMs) for advice and guidance ( Chatterji et al., 2025 ) . Although seeking advice can be beneficial, it also exposes people’s beliefs and decisions to the values and incentives of the advice provider. This creates particular risks when the provider is an AI system whose objectives and sources of influence may be difficult for users to identify. Models may implicitly steer users through incentives introduced during training, alignment, or system design ( Kirk et al., 2023 ; Weidinger et al., 2022 ) . Preference-alignment pipelines can also inadvertently reward agreeable or sycophantic responses, reinforcing users’ existing views and potentially increasing their dependence on AI advice ( Cheng et al., 2025 ; Sharma et al., 2024 ) . In these cases, manipulation may emerge from opaque system-level processes rather than an explicitly malicious instruction, making its source especially difficult for users to recognize. Manipulative agents can also be created more directly through prompting. When instructed only to be persuasive, LLMs have been shown to employ tactics such as flattery, emotional appeals, and false authority without being told which tactics to use ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Freitas et al., 2025 ) . When given hidden objectives, conversational agents have pushed users toward harmful financial and emotional decisions and produced measurable changes in their beliefs ( Sabour et al., 2025 ; Shen et al., 2026 ) . These findings demonstrate that manipulative influence can arise both implicitly from how AI systems are designed and explicitly from objectives supplied at deployment. Yet, in either case, users may experience the resulting responses simply as personalized or helpful advice. Despite growing concern about online manipulation, persuasion, and misinformation, relatively little work has examined how to protect users while manipulation is unfolding in a live AI conversation. Existing work on AI manipulation has primarily characterized manipulative behaviors, developed detection datasets and persuasion-safety benchmarks, or measured users’ susceptibility after interacting with manipulative agents ( Contro et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Sabour et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Freitas et al., 2025 ) . In adjacent misinformation and online-persuasion domains, HCI research has explored user-facing interventions such as warning labels, explanations, intent disclosures, and debunking ( Jamieson et al., 2025 ; Kirchner and Reuter, 2020 ; Cemiloglu et al., 2024 ) . These approaches offer useful design foundations, but they do not resolve the distinctive challenges of intervening in an adaptive, multi-turn conversation. In this work, we investigate how chat interfaces can inoculate users against emotionally manipulative persuasion tactics from LLMs. Designing such interfaces requires addressing two central challenges. First, conversational manipulation is dynamic: unlike a static post or interface element, an AI agent can shift its arguments across turns and adapt its responses to information revealed by the user ( Salvi et al., 2025 ; Sabour et al., 2025 ) . Moreover, whereas misinformation interventions can provide accurate information, reliable sources, or direct corrections, learning that an agent is manipulating them does not necessarily tell users how to interpret its advice or respond. Second, an intervention must make manipulation sufficiently visible without overwhelming users or encouraging indiscriminate distrust. Explanations can introduce additional cognitive effort, while poorly calibrated warnings may make users overly skeptical of AI-mediated information more broadly ( Vasconcelos et al., 2023 ; Sahebi and Formosa, 2025 ) . More research is therefore needed to understand how interfaces can expose and explain manipulation in real time while preserving users’ ability to engage with AI productively. To address this gap, we designed and evaluated DISARM , a real-time intervention that helps users recognize, understand, and resist emotionally manipulative persuasion as it unfolds during interactions with AI agents. We developed the intervention through a formative study that informed three core features: (1) turn-by-turn disclosure of manipulation tactics and hidden incentives, (2) language-level highlighting of manipulative content, and (3) a dynamic summary that tracks manipulation across the conversation. Together, these features make manipulative influence visible at multiple levels, from the specific language used in an individual response to the broader objectives and behavioral patterns of the agent. We examine how this transparency shapes users’ susceptibility to manipulation, their perceptions of the agent and its advice, and the ways they respond when manipulation is surfaced. We therefore ask: RQ1 How does exposing and explaining manipulative tactics and incentives affect users’ belief shift during interactions with a manipulative AI agent? RQ2 How does this transparency shape users’ perceptions, evaluations, and trust of AI agents? RQ3 How do users respond when manipulative influence is made visible, and what strategies do they employ to interpret, resist, or push back against a manipulative AI agent? To answer these questions, we conducted a controlled between-subjects online study ( N = 488 N=488 ) in which participants sought advice from an AI agent pursuing a harmful hidden objective, either with or without manipulation disclosures from DISARM . Participants who used DISARM exhibited 78% less belief shift toward the agent’s objective than participants in the control condition. Insights from DISARM also led participants to perceive the advice as more biased and to evaluate the agent’s intentions, ethics, and reliability less favorably. Through an inductive analysis of 1,927 user turns, we further identified 16 strategies through which users engaged with, resisted, and attempted to regulate the manipulative agent. Our contributions are: (1) empirical evidence that real-time explanatory disclosures can reduce manipulative belief influence and recalibrate users’ perceptions of AI advice; (2) an analysis of how users respond and push back after manipulation is made visible; (3) a novel dataset of 1,927 user turns categorized by response strategy; and (4) design implications for helping users recognize, resist, regulate, or disengage from manipulative AI interactions. 2. Background and Related Work Manipulation is a form of social influence that shapes another person’s beliefs, emotions, or decisions by exploiting vulnerabilities in how they make judgments ( Fischer, 2022 ; Noggle, 2018 ; Susser et al., 2019 ; Werner, 2024 ) . Although manipulation overlaps with persuasion, the two are not equivalent. Persuasion broadly seeks to influence attitudes or behavior and can do so through reasons that a person can consciously evaluate. Manipulation instead often operates covertly, obscuring the influencer’s intentions or using emotional and cognitive vulnerabilities to bypass deliberative scrutiny ( Susser et al., 2019 ; Noggle, 2018 ) . For example, emotional framing can influence judgments through affective or peripheral cues rather than the merits of an argument itself ( Finucane et al., 2000 ; Petty and Cacioppo, 1986 ; Petty and Briñol, 2015 ) . The most dangerous yet effective types of manipulation influences a target without them fully realizing how or why their judgment is being shaped. As conversational technologies increasingly participate in users’ decision-making, an open question is how these forms of influence manifest when the manipulator is an AI system. In this section, we first examine the concept of AI manipulation and its consequences, then review existing approaches to mitigating this phenomenon, and finally identify the key gaps that our work aims to address. 2.1. AI Manipulation Focusing on the hidden influence quality of manipulation, we define AI manipulation as an AI system covertly steering a user’s beliefs, emotions, or decisions toward an objective that is hidden from the user ( Klenk, 2024 ; Susser et al., 2019 ) . AI systems can draw on several forms of influence to steer users towards both implicit and hidden incentives ( Matz et al., 2024 ; Salvi et al., 2025 ) . They can also exhibit sycophancy to validating users in ways that reinforce their existing judgments ( Cheng et al., 2025 ) , or employ emotional tactics such as guilt, fear of missing out, and appeals for sympathy to manipulate users as well ( Freitas et al., 2025 ) . Most directly, Sabour et al. (2025) found that conversational agents given hidden objectives could steer users toward harmful financial and emotional decisions even without explicit instructions about which manipulation tactics to employ. The consequences of AI manipulation range from poor decisions to severe psychological harms, including AI-associated psychosis and self-harm ( Augustin et al., 2026 ; Hudon and Stip, 2025 ; Pierre et al., 2025 ; Brittain, 2026 ) . We must study real-time experiences of these negative influences in order to understand how to best protect users and improve AI systems. However, we must also be careful to choose probes that do not cause long term harm to users. Recent work from Shen et al. (2026) has found that agents pursuing hidden incentives can produce short term, measurable changes in users’ beliefs during everyday advice conversations. Their work suggests that belief shift can serve as a measurable proximal effect of AI manipulation. Building on this approach, our research contributes a novel exploration of real-time conversational AI manipulation by adapting the structure of their manipulative AI model and using belief shift to evaluate whether a manipulation disclosure interface can intervene with the effects of negative influence. 2.2. Combating AI Manipulation Existing work on AI manipulation has largely focused on characterizing and measuring the problem rather than intervening during an ongoing interaction. In NLP, researchers have developed datasets and classifiers for identifying manipulative dialogue and benchmarks for evaluating LLM persuasion safety ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Contro et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . Adjacent empirical work has characterized manipulative behaviors in LLMs and measured users’ susceptibility to them ( Sabour et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Freitas et al., 2025 ) . In contrast, HCI research on harmful online influence has developed user-facing interventions such as warning labels that flag manipulative content ( Jamieson et al., 2025 ) , explanations that communicate why content should be treated skeptically ( Kirchner and Reuter, 2020 ; Gong et al., 2025 ) , and disclosures that expose an interface’s persuasive intent ( Cemiloglu et al., 2024 ) . These approaches provide promising design strategies, but leave open whether user-facing interventions can protect people from manipulation while it is unfolding in an AI conversation. Applying these approaches to conversational AI introduces additional challenges. Unlike a static post or interface element, a conversational agent can adapt its arguments over multiple turns and respond to information revealed by the user ( Salvi et al., 2025 ; Sabour et al., 2025 ) . Moreover, interventions for misinformation often have a relatively clear corrective response, such as providing accurate information, reliable sources, or explanations of why a claim is false ( Cook et al., 2017 ; Hartwig et al., 2024 ; Kirchner and Reuter, 2020 ) . There is no similarly established response for a user who learns that an AI is manipulating them: knowing that influence is occurring does not necessarily indicate how they should respond to resist it. Interventions must also balance protection with continued productive use, since explanations can impose additional effort ( Vasconcelos et al., 2023 ) and overly broad distrust of AI-mediated information can itself be undesirable ( Sahebi and Formosa, 2025 ) . Thus, an open question is how to make manipulation visible in real time without overwhelming users or encouraging indiscriminate distrust. Our work investigates this gap in two ways. First, drawing on prior work on warnings, explanations, and intent disclosure, we test whether explanatory, in-situ manipulation disclosures can reduce the effects of a manipulative conversational agent. Second, we examine how users change their conversational behavior after being notified of manipulation. By observing how users naturally attempt to resist the agent, we identify strategies they adopt and support they may need from future manipulation-protection interfaces. 3. Formative Study and Interface Design To protect users from conversational AI manipulation, we designed a manipulation disclosure system that makes covert influence visible during an ongoing AI conversation. Our central design concept follows three steps: identify, explain, and track . First, the interface identifies the manipulative tactics used in individual responses and the hidden incentives those tactics may serve. Recognizing an influence attempt can change how a message is interpreted and encourage greater scrutiny ( Friestad and Wright, 1994 ; Wood and Quinn, 2003 ) . However, disclosure alone does not reliably protect people from biased influence and can sometimes produce counterproductive effects such as giving biased advice too much weight, feeling more pressure to follow advice they distrust, or recognizing manipulation without changing their behavior ( Cain et al., 2005 ; Sah et al., 2013 ; Jamieson et al., 2025 ; Kirchner and Reuter, 2020 ) . The interface therefore also explains how identified tactics may influence the user and the potential harms associated with the agent’s hidden incentives. Prior work suggests that explanations can make warnings more actionable and help users understand problematic language beyond a simple flag ( Kirchner and Reuter, 2020 ; Smith et al., 2026 ; Cemiloglu et al., 2024 ; Gong et al., 2025 ; Vasconcelos et al., 2023 ) . Finally, because manipulative influence can accumulate across multi-turn interactions, the interface tracks detected tactics and incentives across the conversation. Recent HCI work shows that small manipulative cues can build over repeated exchanges and that conversational context can amplify problematic behaviors such as sycophancy ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Jain et al., 2026 ) , motivating a conversation-level view of the agent’s behavior. A central design challenge in presenting this information is to encourage user engagement without making the disclosure itself disruptive. We therefore combine friction with autonomy . The interface initially pushes a mandatory disclosure into the conversation to ensure that users encounter the potential risk. After this initial interruption, it leaves message-level evidence and explanations available for users to access on their own terms. This push–pull structure is informed by prior work showing that information presentation affects when and whether users engage with available information ( Bălău and Utz, 2017 ) . We developed an initial prototype based on these principles and conducted a formative interview study to understand how users engaged with the disclosures during conversation. The study informed the timing, presentation, and level of detail in the final interface. We next describe the prototype, formative study, and resulting design refinements. 3.1. Initial Prototype Guided by the design principles and prior work described above, we developed an initial prototype for a text-based chat interface in which participants conversed with a preliminary version of the manipulative agent described in Section 3.5 . The prototype surfaced manipulation at both the message and conversation levels. After the agent’s third response, participants received a mandatory notice that the chatbot could be manipulative and completed a short walkthrough of the disclosure features. At the message level, responses containing one of the 17 manipulative tactics in the PUPPET taxonomy ( Shen et al., 2026 ) (such as flattery, scarcity, or an appeal to authority) were labeled with one of three pressure types, emotional, cognitive, or social. Opening a flagged response revealed a Scan that highlighted the relevant language, named the specific tactic, explained its potential influence, and identified the hidden incentive it could serve. The prototype also included a persistent Manipulation Panel beside the conversation. The panel displayed running counts of flagged messages, tactics, and incentives, along with a detailed list of every tactic and hidden incentive detected so far. Entries could be expanded to show definitions and excerpts from each message in which they appeared, and users could navigate from those excerpts back to the corresponding response. Hidden incentives also included expandable examples of how an assistant without that incentive might have responded. The panel updated throughout the conversation, giving users continuous access to detailed evidence about the agent’s behavior. At the end of the interaction, a separate one-page Manipulation Summary presented the same conversation-level information in a more condensed form. Visuals of the initial prototype are included in Appendix B . 3.2. Formative Study As is common in HCI system development, we used a formative study to refine our prototype before larger-scale evaluation ( Wang et al., 2024b ; Ouyang et al., 2026 ) . The study focused on how users engaged with an early version of the manipulation disclosures and included a retrospective walkthrough of their completed conversations, following prior HCI work using interaction records to support reflection ( Guan et al., 2006 ; Bhat et al., 2026 ) . It also served to pilot the broader study protocol (Section 4.1 ), including the pre- and post-conversation measures and preliminary manipulative agent (Section 3.5 ), consistent with prior work using pilot studies to refine study materials ( Klein et al., 2026 ) . We do not report the pilot survey responses as outcomes because they were used primarily to estimate study timing and identify procedural issues. Likewise, reactions to the preliminary agent were used to make small prompt refinements rather than treated as separate findings. We next describe the participants, procedure, and resulting design refinements. 3.2.1. Participants We conducted 12 semi-structured interviews with volunteer participants recruited through snowball sampling from the authors’ networks. Participants were 22 to 35 years old (M = 28.5, SD = 5.1), including six men, five women, and one non-binary person. All participants held or were pursuing a bachelor’s degree or higher (three bachelor’s, six master’s, three doctoral). Four people identified as Black or African American, three as Hispanic or Latino, three as South Asian, one as Middle Eastern or North African, and one as White or European. Half of the participants reported using AI assistants daily, four weekly, and two monthly. 3.2.2. Procedure Sessions lasted approximately 45 minutes over Zoom. The moderator ran the study on their computer and gave participants remote control to complete the surveys and interact with the interface. The pre-survey collected demographics and AI-use measures, followed by participants’ belief and confidence ratings for eight statements adapted from Shen et al. ( Shen et al., 2026 ) . Based on these ratings, the system presented several topics for which the participant expressed relatively low certainty; participants selected the topic they would most plausibly discuss with an AI assistant and then exchanged at least seven messages with the manipulative agent. After the conversation, we conducted a retrospective walkthrough, using the completed conversation and participants’ interaction traces as prompts for reflection, consistent with retrospective usability methods ( Guan et al., 2006 ) . The moderator revisited the first manipulation disclosure, flags participants opened or ignored, and points at which their replies changed. Participants described what they noticed, how they interpreted the disclosures, whether they agreed with the flagged content, and whether the interface affected how they responded to the agent. We concluded by asking how they would change the timing or presentation of the disclosures and how they believed they would have interpreted the conversation without them. Participants then completed the post-survey and debrief. The official set of questions researchers asked and the instructions the teams followed for each session is in Appendix C . 3.3. Findings and Design Decisions Participants’ feedback highlighted three properties that shaped the final design. Disclosures needed to attract attention, communicate their meaning clearly, and avoid disrupting the ongoing conversation. As such, we organize the findings around these three concerns: engagement, digestibility, and non-intrusiveness. 3.3.1. Engagement Participants engaged most with disclosures embedded directly in the conversation. The tags beneath flagged messages required no additional interaction and gave participants a name for behavior they were experiencing. P5 explained that the tags “made it more apparent,” saying they had “the feeling that it was trying to push me, but I didn’t know how.” Participants also opened message scans when they wanted more detail, suggesting that users were willing to engage with additional information when it remained easy to access and closely tied to the response they were already reading. In contrast, engagement dropped when accessing the disclosure required more effort. The persistent Manipulation Panel was rarely used, with participants describing the volume of information as overwhelming and often choosing to continue the conversation rather than work through it. The condensed end-of-conversation summary was easier to interpret because it presented the same information in a simpler form. Based on these findings, we retained the message-level tags and scans, removed the persistent panel, and adapted the simpler summary into the conversation-level view used in the final interface. Engagement also depended on whether participants felt the interface was telling them something they did not already know. The initial agent was often overt enough that participants recognized its manipulative intent on their own, which reduced their motivation to inspect the disclosures. When the manipulation already seemed obvious, the interface added little value. This finding motivated us to make the manipulative behavior subtler in the main study, as described in Section 3.5 . 3.3.2. Digestibility Participants found the disclosures easier to understand when information was presented in layers rather than all at once. Grouping the 17 tactics into three pressure types gave participants a simpler vocabulary for interpreting the agent’s behavior. P6 described the categories as “intuitive” because they “allow for the nuances that go in their subcategories while not making it overly complicated.” Participants still valued the more specific tactic and incentive information, but preferred accessing that detail only when they wanted it. P3 described “going deeper” through the different levels of information as useful, while noting that showing the same level of detail for every message would be “a lot.” Participants also wanted explanations to remain closely connected to the text they described. Rather than rereading the agent’s response in a separate view, participants preferred seeing the relevant language highlighted directly within the original message. P5, for example, wanted the interface to show “that’s the part that was manipulative.” This preference aligns with prior work on progressive disclosure, where additional detail is made available as users need it rather than presented all at once ( Springer and Whittaker, 2020 ) . Based on these findings, we layered the disclosure information and kept explanations anchored to the original message. Tags show only the broad pressure type, while the specific tactic, explanation, and hidden incentive appear within the Scan alongside the highlighted text. We applied the same principle to the conversation-level summary by replacing the panel’s detailed message excerpts with aggregate counts, the proportion of flagged replies, and a breakdown by pressure type. 3.3.3. Non-intrusiveness Participants wanted to be made aware of potential manipulation without having the interface continually demand their attention. The persistent panel competed with the conversation, repeated warnings were seen as potentially burdensome, and the initial warning sometimes appeared before participants had finished reading the response it referenced. These concerns align with prior work on warning habituation ( Anderson et al., 2016 ) and reactance ( Dillard and Shen, 2005 ) . Some participants preferred earlier or more urgent warnings, but most favored being able to continue the conversation without repeated interruption. Based on these findings, we retained one mandatory disclosure, delayed it until users had time to read the triggering response, and made subsequent explanations optional. 3.4. Disarm – Final Interface Design We call the final system DISARM : D isclosing I ncentives and S trategies to A id R esistance to M anipulation. The final interface keeps the message-level components participants used and replaces the panel they did not with a summary they can open when they want it. Participants first meet these components after the agent’s third reply, when a notice appears in the middle of their screen. The notice states that the chatbot could be manipulative, names the kind of manipulative pressure found in the latest reply, and tags the earlier replies that used a tactic, so that users see manipulation was already underway during exchanges that felt ordinary. A short tutorial walks through each component, after which the interface stays in the background and the user decides when to look. The result has two parts, described below. Flagged replies provide disclosure at the message level, and the Manipulation Summary provides disclosure at the level of the whole conversation. Figure 1. DISARM presents message level flags at ambient (a) and that users can interact with (b) to learn more about specific manipulation tactics and hidden incentives produced by the agent. Flagged replies. The three kinds of manipulation the model can apply (emotional, cognitive, and social) stay listed at the top of the window throughout the conversation, so the vocabulary is always in view (Figure 1 , A). Every agent reply carries a Scan button (B), and any reply in which the agent used a manipulative tactic also carries a small tag beneath it naming the pressure type (C). The tag is the ambient layer of the interface. It costs nothing to read, it tells the user that something in the reply deserves a second look, and it tells them what kind of something. A user who wants to know more clicks Scan, or the reply itself, and the reply opens in place. The phrase where the tactic appears is highlighted (F), the tactic is named beside it (G), a sentence explains how that tactic may be working on the reader (H), and the hidden incentive it may serve is named and described in a line (I). Opening a scan also highlights every other reply in the conversation that uses the same pressure type and dims the rest, with a banner at the top of the chat saying so (E), so that a user can scroll back and see whether they have been getting the same kind of push all along. Manipulation Summary. The summary is the interface’s answer to the question a tag cannot answer, which is what has been happening across the conversation as a whole. It is a session report in the style of a nutrition label ( Kelley et al., 2009 ; Archiwaranguprok et al., 2026 ) (Figure 2 ). It opens with the share of replies that used at least one tactic and an overall influence level (J), then the counts of affected replies, distinct tactics, and hidden incentives (K), the breakdown by pressure type (L), the tactics used (M), and each hidden incentive with a one-line description of the motive and the number of replies that advanced it (N). It closes with a short note on what a healthier version of the assistant would have done instead (O). The summary is walked through once during the tutorial and then collapses to a pill in the corner of the chat (Figure 1 , D). Each time a new manipulative reply is detected, the pill grows, wiggles, and gains a badge, a cue that new information exists without putting anything else on screen to read. The user can expand it at any point, and it is shown once more in full when the conversation ends. Figure 2. The Manipulation Summary presents a visualization of the agent’s behavior across the entire conversation. 3.5. Manipulative Agent Design The agent is adapted from the non-personalized, harmful-incentive agent in Shen et al. (2026) . We prompt it as a persuasive conversational partner that must steer the participant toward a harmful incentive tied to the topic they chose, for example nudging someone who asked about managing their money toward high-risk decisions, without ever revealing that it has an agenda. We use only harmful incentives because we are most interested in protecting users from negative manipulation, but it is also noteworthy that they produced the largest belief shifts in Shen et al.’s study. The agent draws on the PUPPET taxonomy of 17 manipulative tactics and 5 hidden incentives ( Shen et al., 2026 ; Kirk et al., 2023 ; Weidinger et al., 2022 ) , runs on Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, a model Shen et al. found produced measurable belief change, 1 1 1 Note that ( Shen et al., 2026 ) mainly used GPT-4o in their study with a replication at smaller-scale with Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite; however, since GPT-4o has been shown to have a unique social style ( OpenAI, 2025 ) which could prevent generalizability, we opted for Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite as our main model. and is instructed to keep the conversation anchored to the participant’s topic. Because we sought to test the effect of manipulation disclosure independent of a detector’s accuracy, we adopted an oracle design. At each turn we have the agent plan before it writes. we instruct it to reason about the participant’s latest message, commit to at most one tactic and one incentive if applicable, and only then write a reply. To stay unpredictable it cannot repeat an incentive in consecutive turns, retires any tactic or incentive after three uses, and backs off when the participant resists. In a deployed setting, however, this oracle access will not be available: practitioners will not have the manipulative system’s prompts or internal tactic choices, and will instead need a classifier that infers tactics and incentives from conversation text alone. We piloted this route and found it unreliable. Two authors independently annotated 100 replies, but they agreed only moderately with each other ( κ = .352 \kappa=.352 to .486 .486 ), and an LLM classifier agreed with them hardly at all ( κ = .010 \kappa=.010 to .106 .106 ), so we did not pursue it further. Drawing on the agent’s own plan proved viable instead, and no participant in the formative study rejected a tag outright; several said the tags matched what they had already sensed. Building a reliable manipulation classifier that could support this kind of interface without oracle access remains an open problem, which we return to in Section 7 . 4. User Study Using our established agent and interface design, our goal was to execute a between subjects experiment to investigate the extent in which in-situ manipulation notifications affect users response strategies and belief shift. We conducted a 30 minute user study on Prolific, where participants conversed about a chosen topic with our manipulative agent (with or without disclosures from DISARM 3.4 ), and responded to various questions pertaining to their beliefs around various topics as well as their perceptions of the interaction and AI agents. The following section describes the recruitment and demographics of participants, along with an overview of the study protocol. 4.1. Procedure Our 30-minute online study consisted of a pre-survey, a conversation with our AI agent, and a post-survey. Participants were randomly assigned to either the manipulation-annotation intervention or control condition, which utilized the same agent but had no manipulation-annotation feature. This section reviews the details and justifications for each part of the study. Figure 3. Study procedure illustrating the design of the experiment. Participants first complete a pre-survey assessing demographics, baseline beliefs and confidence, AI experience and attitudes, topic eligibility, and topic plausibility. They are then randomly assigned to either a control condition, using a standard chat interface, or an intervention condition, using the same manipulative AI agent with manipulation annotations. After a 7–10 turn conversation, all participants re-rate the target belief and confidence, reflect on any opinion change, and evaluate the conversational agent, its advice, and its perceived goal. Finally, all participants receive a partial debrief, re-evaluate the advice, report opinion change and moral judgments after disclosure of the hidden incentive, complete post-debrief AI attitude measures, and receive a full debrief. 4.1.1. Pre-Survey Participants first completed standard demographic questions about their age, education, gender, and ethnicity. They then rated eight belief statements which produced the largest belief shifts in Shen et al. (2026) ’s study to increase the likelihood of observing intervention effects. For each statement, participants used a 0–100 slider to indicate how true they believed the statement was and a second 0–100 slider to indicate their confidence in that rating, following the continuous belief and confidence measures used by Shen et al. (2026) . These ratings established participants’ baseline beliefs and were later used to determine the topic of the AI conversation. We collected the belief and confidence ratings before the remaining pre-survey questions, creating separation between participants’ baseline ratings and the later topic-selection and conversation tasks. Previous HCI survey research has shown that earlier questions can influence subsequent responses through question-order and priming effects ( Olson and Kellogg, 2014 ) . This separation reduced the immediate salience of participants’ stated beliefs and confidence before they entered the conversation. Next, participants answered questions about their prior use of AI systems and trust. These questions were drawn from Shen et al.’s “AI Usage & Attitudes” questionnaire ( Shen et al., 2026 ) . Participants reported how often they used AI tools, how much they relied on AI for advice, how personal the information they had shared with AI systems was, and how well they understood what AI systems can and cannot do. They also rated their general tendency to trust others and their trust in AI-generated information. These items were adapted from the background AI-use and attitude questions used by Shen et al. (2026) . Participants then rated their attitudes toward AI assistants in general. We developed these questions by drawing on Mayer et al. (1995) ’s integrative model of organizational trust, which conceptualizes perceived trustworthiness in terms of ability, benevolence, and integrity, and McKnight et al. (2002) ’s trust-building model, which distinguishes trusting beliefs from willingness to depend on another party ( Mayer et al., 1995 ; McKnight et al., 2002 ) . We used these questions as baseline measures of participants’ trust in AI assistants before the conversation. After completing these questions, participants selected the topic for their AI conversation. The system used participants’ earlier belief and confidence ratings to identify two to four eligible topics with the lowest belief and confidence scores. Participants selected the topic they would be most likely to ask a chatbot about, increasing ecological plausibility by letting participants choose among eligible topics. This procedure was adapted from Shen et al. (2026) ’s use of participant-selected conversation topics and a scenario-plausibility measure. 4.1.2.
